sentences.text: Nuthetes is a coelurosaurian theropod dinosaur whose genus name means "one who admonishes" or "a monitor," referencing the similarity of its teeth to modern monitor lizards.
The species name destructor means "destroyer," referring to teeth adapted for piercing and cutting prey in an animal estimated to be the size of a Bengal monitor.
Fossils once attributed to Nuthetes were later identified in 2002 as osteoderms from a turtle, not the dinosaur.
The holotype was thought to be lost until it was rediscovered in the 1970s at the Dorset County Museum.
Nuthetes destructor was named and described by Richard Owen in 1854.
The holotype was collected by amateur paleontologist Charles Willcox from the Feather Quarry near Durlston Bay.
If Nuthetes was a dromaeosaurid, it would have been a small predator.
Richard Owen originally classified Nuthetes as a lizard and later as a crocodilian, but Richard Lydekker was the first to correctly identify Nuthetes as a dinosaur in 1888.

A 2002 re-examination by Angela Milner suggested Nuthetes most likely belonged to a subadult dromaeosaurid, while Steve Sweetman concluded that Nuthetes destructor is a velociraptorine dromaeosaurid based on an examination of five fossil teeth specimens.
Nuthetes lived between 143.1 and 137.05 million years ago during the Berriasian stage.
Fossils of Nuthetes have been found in the Early Cretaceous (middle Berriasian) Lulworth Formation in England and the Angeac-Charente bonebed in France.

Researchers Rauhut, Milner, and Moore-Fay (2010) noted the similarity between Nuthetes teeth and those of the basal tyrannosauroid Proceratosaurus, suggesting caution in classifying isolated teeth as dromaeosaurids.
